claim: Aged tendons have disrupted homeostasis, increased injury risk, and impaired healing capacity.
source: Aged tendons have disrupted homeostasis, increased injury risk, and impaired healing capacity.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about tendon aging.

claim: Scx-DTR recapitulates many aspects of tendon aging including comparable declines in cellularity, alterations in ECM structure, organization, and composition.
source: Scx-DTR recapitulates many aspects of tendon aging including comparable declines in cellularity, alterations in ECM structure, organization, and composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing Scx-DTR and aged tendons.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing demonstrated a conserved decline in tenocytes associated with ECM biosynthesis in aged and Scx-DTR tendons.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing demonstrated a conserved decline in tenocytes associated with ECM biosynthesis in aged and Scx-DTR tendons, identifying the requirement for Scleraxis-lineage cells during homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Scleraxis-lineage cells are required during homeostasis.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing demonstrated a conserved decline in tenocytes associated with ECM biosynthesis in aged and Scx-DTR tendons, identifying the requirement for Scleraxis-lineage cells during homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the effects of Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion.

claim: Aged tenocytes become pro-inflammatory and lose proteostasis.
source: Aged tenocytes become pro-inflammatory and lose proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing gene expression patterns in aged tenocytes.

claim: Tenocytes from Scx-DTR tendons demonstrate enhanced remodeling capacity.
source: In contrast, tenocytes from Scx-DTR tendons demonstrate enhanced remodeling capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing gene expression patterns in Scx-DTR tenocytes.

claim: Scleraxis is the most well-characterized tendon marker.
source: Scleraxis, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, is the most well-characterized tendon marker (Schweitzer et al., 2001; Murchison et al., 2007; Pryce et al., 2009) and is required for normal tendon development (Schweitzer et al., 2001; Murchison et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Scleraxis is required for normal tendon development.
source: Scleraxis, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, is the most well-characterized tendon marker (Schweitzer et al., 2001; Murchison et al., 2007; Pryce et al., 2009) and is required for normal tendon development (Schweitzer et al., 2001; Murchison et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Scleraxis-lineage cells are the predominant population during adult mouse homeostasis.
source: Recent studies from our group and others have demonstrated the presence of multiple tendon resident cell populations, with Scleraxis-lineage (ScxLin) cells being the predominant population during adult mouse homeostasis (Best et al., 2021; De Micheli et al., 2020; Best and Loiselle, 2019; Kendal et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tendon homeostasis is maintained via ongoing turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins during adulthood.
source: During adulthood, tendon homeostasis is maintained via ongoing turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins (Samiric et al., 2004a; Samiric et al., 2004b; Choi et al., 2020; Heinemeier et al., 2016; Rees et al., 2009; Korcari et al., 2021b; Neidlin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homeostatic disruptions can lead to the development of tendon pathologies such as tendinopathy.
source: Homeostatic disruptions can lead to the development of tendon pathologies such as tendinopathy, which are characterized by significant pain and permanent decline in tissue performance (Millar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Natural aging is associated with impaired tendon homeostasis.
source: While repetitive loading in sports or occupational contexts disrupt homeostasis, natural aging is also associated with impaired tendon homeostasis (Pardes et al., 2017; Connizzo et al., 2013; Peffers et al., 2014; Gehwolf et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Kostrominova and Brooks, 2013; Marqueti et al., 2018; Korcari et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tendinopathy prevalence increases substantially with age.
source: Tendinopathy prevalence increases substantially with age (Riel et al., 2019), making aging a key risk factor for loss of tendon health.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Aging is a key risk factor for loss of tendon health.
source: Tendinopathy prevalence increases substantially with age (Riel et al., 2019), making aging a key risk factor for loss of tendon health.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited data on tendinopathy prevalence.

claim: Depletion of ScxLin cells results in a relatively rapid loss of ECM structural and organizational integrity of the flexor digitorum longus (FDL) tendon.
source: We have previously shown that depletion of ScxLin cells results in a relatively rapid loss of ECM structural and organizational integrity of the flexor digitorum longus (FDL) tendon (Best et al., 2021), suggesting that ScxLin cells are required to maintain tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: ScxLin cells are required to maintain tendon homeostasis.
source: We have previously shown that depletion of ScxLin cells results in a relatively rapid loss of ECM structural and organizational integrity of the flexor digitorum longus (FDL) tendon (Best et al., 2021), suggesting that ScxLin cells are required to maintain tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results cited.

claim: The initial ECM organizational changes that occur with ScxLin cell depletion mimic those that occur during natural aging.
source: Moreover, while the initial ECM organizational changes that occur with ScxLin cell depletion mimic those that occur during natural aging (Connizzo et al., 2013; Gehwolf et al., 2016; Dunkman et al., 2013; Ippolito et al., 1980; Connizzo et al., 2016), it is unknown whether sustained ScxLin cell depletion in young mice may induce an aged tendon phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on aging and the authors' prior work on depletion.

claim: At 3 M and 6 M post-depletion, there was a respective 57.44% (p<0.0001) and 56.21% (p<0.0001) reduction in total tendon cell density in DTR tendons relative to the WT littermates.
source: At 3 M and 6 M post-depletion, there was a respective 57.44% (p<0.0001) and 56.21% (p<0.0001) reduction in total tendon cell density in DTR tendons relative to the WT littermates (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: By 9 M post-depletion (12 M of age), there was an age-related decrease in tendon cell density in WT such that no significant differences in cell density were observed between DTR and WT (p>0.05).
source: By 9 M post-depletion (12 M of age), there was an age-related decrease in tendon cell density in WT such that no significant differences in cell density were observed between DTR and WT (p>0.05) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: At 10 M in C57Bl/6 J tendons, cellularity was decreased with a 31.62% (p<0.0001) decline in cell density compared to 6 M old WT, and a 32.06% decrease (p<0.0001) compared to 9 M old WT tendons.
source: Consistent with the progressive decline in cellularity in WT tendons, cellularity was further decreased at 10 M in C57Bl/6 J tendons, with a 31.62% (p<0.0001) decline in cell density compared to 6 M old WT, and a 32.06% decrease (p<0.0001) compared to 9 M old WT tendons (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: At 13 and 31 M, C57Bl/6 J FDL tendons showed a 43.19% (p<0.001) and a 44.42% (p<0.001) decrease in total cell density compared to 10 M old C57Bl/6 J FDL tendons, respectively.
source: At 13 and 31 M, C57Bl/6 J FDL tendons showed a 43.19% (p<0.001) and a 44.42% (p<0.001) decrease in total cell density compared to 10 M old C57Bl/6 J FDL tendons, respectively (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: 6 M old DTR tendons (3 M post-depletion) exhibited a cell density almost identical to 13 M and 31 M old C57Bl/6 J tendons (p>0.05).
source: Intriguingly, 6 M old DTR tendons (3 M post-depletion) exhibited a cell density almost identical to 13 M and 31 M old C57Bl/6 J tendons (p>0.05) (Figure 1D and E), suggesting that with Scleraxis-lineage depletion, young tendons exhibit the same cell density as old (12 M) and geriatric (31 M) tendons (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: With Scleraxis-lineage depletion, young tendons exhibit the same cell density as old (12 M) and geriatric (31 M) tendons.
source: Intriguingly, 6 M old DTR tendons (3 M post-depletion) exhibited a cell density almost identical to 13 M and 31 M old C57Bl/6 J tendons (p>0.05) (Figure 1D and E), suggesting that with Scleraxis-lineage depletion, young tendons exhibit the same cell density as old (12 M) and geriatric (31 M) tendons (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the quantitative data showing similar cell densities.

claim: Quantification of collagen dispersion via SHG imaging demonstrated significant increases in dispersion (loss of organization) at 3 M (39.82%, p<0.05), 6 M (41.04%, p<0.01), and 9 M (24.53%, p<0.05) post-DT, relative to WT littermates.
source: Quantification of collagen dispersion via SHG imaging demonstrated significant increases in dispersion (loss of organization) at 3 M (39.82%, p<0.05), 6 M (41.04%, p<0.01), and 9 M (24.53%, p<0.05) post-DT, relative to WT littermates (Figure 1F and G), indicative of impairments in tissue structure and organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from SHG imaging presented in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Geriatric 31 M old C57Bl/6 J tendons exhibited a significant increase in collagen fibril dispersion compared to 10 M (79.3%; p<0.0001) and 13 M (81.47%, p<0.0001) C57Bl/6 J tendons.
source: Geriatric 31 M old C57Bl/6 J tendons exhibited a significant increase in collagen fibril dispersion compared to 10 M (79.3%; p<0.0001) and 13 M (81.47%, p<0.0001) C57Bl/6 J tendons (Figure 1H1), suggesting aging-induced impairments in tendon structure and organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from SHG imaging presented in Figure 1H.

claim: 3 M post-DT (6 M old) DTR tendons showed a 45.8% (p<0.01) and a 47.63% (p<0.01) increase in collagen dispersion compared to 10 M and 13 M C57BL/6 J tendons, respectively.
source: In contrast, 3 M post-DT (6 M old) DTR tendons showed a 45.8% (p<0.01) and a 47.63% (p<0.01) increase in collagen dispersion compared to 10 M and 13 M C57BL/6 J tendons, respectively (Figure 1H1), suggesting that young DTR tendons recapitulate several aspects of age-related deficits in tissue organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from SHG imaging presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Young DTR tendons recapitulate several aspects of age-related deficits in tissue organization.
source: In contrast, 3 M post-DT (6 M old) DTR tendons showed a 45.8% (p<0.01) and a 47.63% (p<0.01) increase in collagen dispersion compared to 10 M and 13 M C57BL/6 J tendons, respectively (Figure 1H1), suggesting that young DTR tendons recapitulate several aspects of age-related deficits in tissue organization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the quantitative data showing similar increases in collagen dispersion.

claim: Geriatric 31 M old C57BL/6 J tendons had a significantly higher collagen fibril dispersion (+23.02%, p<0.05) compared to 3 M post-DT (6 M old) DTR tendons.
source: However, geriatric 31 M old C57BL/6 J tendons still had a significantly higher collagen fibril dispersion (+23.02%, p<0.05) compared to 3 M post-DT (6 M old) DTR tendons (Figure 1H1), potentially suggesting further degeneration during advanced aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from SHG imaging presented in Figure 1H.

claim: At 3 M post-depletion, 30 proteins were significantly different between the DTR and WT groups.
source: At 3 M post-depletion, 30 proteins were significantly different between the DTR and WT groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: ECM proteins were the most decreased category in DTR tendons, accounting for 26.7% of the total proteins.
source: ECM proteins were the most decreased category in DTR tendons, accounting for 26.7% of the total proteins. (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Functional enrichment analysis of all the downregulated proteins demonstrated that ECM-related molecular functions and cellular components were significantly impaired with depletion.
source: Functional enrichment analysis of all the downregulated proteins demonstrated that ECM-related molecular functions and cellular components were significantly impaired with depletion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of proteomic data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Eleven ECM proteins were decreased in DTR tendons.
source: Eleven ECM proteins were decreased in DTR tendons (Figure 2D), and they were classified as proteoglycans (PG) (36.4%), glycoproteins (GP) (36.4%), ECM regulators (18.2%), and ECM-affiliated proteins (9.1%) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: 72.8% of the decreased ECM proteins in DTR tendons were high turnover rate glycoproteins and proteoglycans including CHAD, COCH, and KERA.
source: Strikingly, 72.8% of these ECM proteins were high turnover rate glycoproteins and proteoglycans including CHAD, COCH, and KERA (Samiric et al., 2004a; Choi et al., 2020; Heinemeier et al., 2016; Tam et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data and citations to prior literature on protein turnover rates.

claim: With natural aging, 25 proteins were significantly different between the aged (12 M) and young (6 M) WT tendons.
source: With natural aging, 25 proteins were significantly different between the aged (12 M) and young (6 M) WT tendons (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: 28.6% of downregulated proteins in 12 M tendons were ECM proteins.
source: Classification of all downregulated proteins in 12 M tendons determined that 28.6% were ECM proteins (Figure 2G) and functional enrichment analysis also showed that ECM-related molecular functions and cellular components were significantly impaired (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2G.

claim: A total of nine decreased ECM proteins were identified in 12 M WT tendons, relative to 6 M WT.
source: A total of nine decreased ECM proteins were identified in 12 M WT tendons, relative to 6 M WT (Figure 2I), and classified as proteoglycans (22.2%), glycoproteins (22.2%), ECM regulators (33.3%), and collagens (22.2%) (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2I.

claim: The majority of the decreased ECM molecules in aged tendons have a high turnover rate.
source: The majority of the above ECM molecules have a high turnover rate, similar to the findings for the 3 M post-depletion timepoints (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proteomic data and comparison to the depletion model.

claim: The proteomes of aged (12 M old) WT tendons vs young (6 M old) DTR were nearly identical.
source: Finally, the proteomes of aged (12 M old) WT tendons vs young (6 M old) DTR were nearly identical (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Four ECM molecules (COCH, CHAD, KERA, and ACAN) were consistently downregulated with both natural aging and Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion.
source: Based on these analyses, we identified four ECM molecules (COCH, CHAD, KERA, and ACAN) that were consistently downregulated with both natural aging and Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion (Figure 2M), and demonstrated a decrease in the proportion of Coch + and Chad + cells in 6 M old DTR and 21 M old B6 tendons using single-cell RNA sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic and single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: There was a decrease in the proportion of Coch + and Chad + cells in 6 M old DTR and 21 M old B6 tendons.
source: Based on these analyses, we identified four ECM molecules (COCH, CHAD, KERA, and ACAN) that were consistently downregulated with both natural aging and Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion (Figure 2M), and demonstrated a decrease in the proportion of Coch + and Chad + cells in 6 M old DTR and 21 M old B6 tendons using single-cell RNA sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was a significant decrease of tendon elastic modulus with both depletion and natural aging.
source: Considering the substantial changes in ECM organization and composition, we also assessed the impact of Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion and natural aging on tendon mechanical integrity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D) and while there were no major changes in CSA (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B) and stiffness (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), there was a significant decrease of tendon elastic modulus with both depletion and natural aging (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by biomechanical testing data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Seven cell types with distinct transcriptomic signatures were identified in the integrated dataset, including tendon fibroblasts (tenocytes), epitenon cells, endothelial, nerve, and muscle cells, macrophages, and T cells.
source: In the integrated dataset, seven cell types with distinct transcriptomic signatures were identified, including tendon fibroblasts (tenocytes), epitenon cells, endothelial, nerve, and muscle cells, macrophages, and T cells (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 6 M DTR and 21 M B6 tendons had a decrease in the total number of tenocytes captured compared to 6 M WT.
source: Consistent with cellularity quantification (Figure 1), 6 M DTR and 21 M B6 tendons had a decrease in the total number of tenocytes captured compared to 6 M WT (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Tenocytes in the 6 M WT group express genes related primarily to ECM biosynthetic process and secondary to ECM organization.
source: Tenocytes in the 6 M WT group express genes related primarily to ECM biosynthetic process and secondary to ECM organization such as Col1a1, Col1a2, Tnxb, Coch, Col11a2, and Fbln1.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing gene expression patterns.

claim: 6 M WT tenocytes are broadly characterized as ECM biosynthetic and ECM organizational.
source: Based on FEA, 6 M WT tenocytes are broadly characterized as ECM biosynthetic ('translation', 'macromolecule biosynthetic process', 'collagen metabolic process') and ECM organizational ('ECM organization', 'homeostatic process', 'collagen fibril organization')(Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Both DTR and aged tenocytes exhibited a decrease in processes related to ECM biosynthesis.
source: Consistent with our proteomics findings, broadly, both DTR and aged tenocytes exhibited a decrease in processes related to ECM biosynthesis such as 'translation', 'biosynthetic process', 'cell and macromolecule biosynthetic process' (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3F-I.

claim: Tissue resident macrophages from aged (21 M B6 tendons) demonstrate similar shifts in biological processes, relative to 6 M WT cells, including enrichment for functions associated with 'protein refolding', and 'response to unfolded proteins'.
source: Interestingly, tissue resident macrophages from aged (21 M B6 tendons) demonstrate similar shifts in biological processes, relative to 6 M WT cells, including enrichment for functions associated with 'protein refolding', and 'response to unfolded proteins' (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: With both depletion and aging, tenocytes 1 were decreased to almost identical levels, with a 75.18% decrease with depletion and a 78.9% decrease with aging.
source: With both depletion and aging, we found that tenocytes 1 were decreased to almost identical levels. Specifically, tenocytes 1 subpopulation exhibited a 75.18% decrease with depletion and a 78.9% decrease with aging (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 4B-E.

claim: Tenocytes 1 express biological processes related to ECM biosynthesis and immune response.
source: FEA analysis demonstrated that tenocytes 1 express biological processes related to ECM biosynthesis ('biosynthetic process', 'collagen biosynthetic' and 'collagen metabolic process') and immune response ('inflammatory' and 'immune response', 'response to IL1', 'T cell activation') (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Gbp2 is a specific marker of tenocytes 1.
source: Finally, we identified Gbp2 as a specific marker of tenocytes 1 (Figure 4J) and found that with both depletion and natural aging there was a decrease in Gbp2+ + compared to the 6 M WT (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: With both depletion and natural aging there was a decrease in Gbp2+ cells compared to the 6 M WT.
source: Finally, we identified Gbp2 as a specific marker of tenocytes 1 (Figure 4J) and found that with both depletion and natural aging there was a decrease in Gbp2+ + compared to the 6 M WT (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: Staining for GBP2 protein showed a 58.66% (p<0.0001) and a 44.54% (p<0.0001) decrease in GBP2+ cells with depletion and natural aging relative to the 6 M WT group.
source: Staining for GBP2 protein validated our scRNAseq results and showed a 58.66% (p<0.0001) and a 44.54% (p<0.0001) decrease in GBP2+ + with depletion and natural aging relative to the 6 M WT group (Figure 4K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4K and L.

claim: The consistent loss of ECM biosynthetic tenocytes 1 in young DTR and aged groups is the main driver for impaired tendon homeostasis.
source: Taken together, our scRNAseq results demonstrate that the consistent loss of ECM biosynthetic tenocytes 1 in young DTR and aged groups is the main driver for impaired tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the single-cell RNA sequencing data showing the loss of tenocytes 1.

claim: Tenocytes in the 6 M DTR group express genes related to ECM organization, development and remodeling.
source: Broadly, tenocytes in the 6 M DTR group express genes related ECM organization, development and remodeling such as Edil3, Mmp2, Col5a1 and Fn1.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing gene expression patterns.

claim: 6 M DTR tenocytes are characterized as specialized cells for ECM organization and remodeling.
source: Based on FEA, 6 M DTR tenocytes are characterized as specialized cells for ECM organization and remodeling ('ECM organization', 'extracellular structure organization' 'supramolecular fiber organization', and 'tissue remodeling').
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Tenocytes from 21 M B6 mice express genes related to hallmarks of aging like loss of proteostasis and inflammaging.
source: In contrast, tenocytes from 21 M B6 mice express genes related to hallmarks of aging like loss of proteostasis (Ppp1r15a, Hspa8, Hsp90aa1, Hspa5, Hspb1, Hspa1, Hspa1b, and Dnajb9) and inflammaging (Il6, Stat3, Tnfaip3, Cxcl12, and Bcl3).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing gene expression patterns.

claim: FEA of 21 M B6 tenocytes demonstrated processes related to 'response to stress', 'response to unfolded protein', 'T cell and leukocyte activation', 'TNF and IL1 production', and 'aging'.
source: Indeed, FEA of 21 M B6 tenocytes demonstrated processes related to 'response to stress', 'response to unfolded protein', 'T cell and leukocyte activation', 'TNF and IL1 production', and 'aging' (Figure 3F1).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3I.

claim: In the DTR group there was a retention of tenocytes 2, while this population was decreased by 96.2% in the aged WT tendon relative to the young WT.
source: Further analysis showed that in the DTR group there was a retention of tenocytes 2, while this population was decreased by 96.2% in the aged WT tendon relative to the young WT (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 4B-E.

claim: Tenocytes 2 express genes that give rise to ECM proteins such as Mmp2, Lum, Col1a1, Col3a1, Col11a1, and Mfap5.
source: Tenocytes 2 express genes that give rise to ECM proteins such as Mmp2, Lum, Col1a1, Col3a1, Col11a1, and Mfap5.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing gene expression patterns.

claim: Tenocytes 2 exhibit functions related to ECM organization and wound healing.
source: FEA demonstrated biological processes such as 'ECM and collagen fibril organization', 'supramolecular fiber organization', 'cell adhesion', and 'wound healing', suggesting that tenocytes 2 exhibit functions related to ECM organization and wound healing (Figure 4F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: Divergent retention of tenocytes in DTR and aged tendons might dictate divergent healing responses after injury.
source: Taken together, these divergent retention of tenocytes in DTR and aged tendons might dictate divergent healing responses after injury.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed differences in tenocyte populations.

claim: In DTR compared to WT tendons, tenocytes 1 exhibited a total of 413 DEG.
source: In DTR compared to WT tendons, tenocytes 1 exhibited a total of 413 DEG (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Tenocytes 1 in the 6 M WT group exhibited processes such as 'translation', 'macromolecule biosynthetic process', 'structure morphogenesis'.
source: FEA revealed that tenocytes 1 in the 6 M WT group exhibited processes such as 'translation', 'macromolecule biosynthetic process', 'structure morphogenesis', while in the 6 M DTR group, tenocytes 1 exhibited processes such as 'cell migration', 'ECM organization', and 'wound healing' (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Tenocytes 1 in the 6 M DTR group exhibited processes such as 'cell migration', 'ECM organization', and 'wound healing'.
source: FEA revealed that tenocytes 1 in the 6 M WT group exhibited processes such as 'translation', 'macromolecule biosynthetic process', 'structure morphogenesis', while in the 6 M DTR group, tenocytes 1 exhibited processes such as 'cell migration', 'ECM organization', and 'wound healing' (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Young WT tenocytes 1 exhibited processes such as 'collagen biosynthesis', 'ECM organization', and 'immune cell chemotaxis'.
source: In contrast, looking at age-related programmatic shifts of tenocytes 1 (Figure 5F–H), while young WT tenocytes 1 exhibited processes such as 'collagen biosynthesis', 'ECM organization', and 'immune cell chemotaxis' (Figure 5I), aged tenocytes 1 exhibited processes related to potential indicators of aging hallmarks such as loss of proteostasis 'response to unfolded protein', 'protein refolding', and 'inflammaging' 'T cell activation', 'immune response' (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5I.

claim: Aged tenocytes 1 exhibited processes related to potential indicators of aging hallmarks such as loss of proteostasis 'response to unfolded protein', 'protein refolding', and 'inflammaging' 'T cell activation', 'immune response'.
source: In contrast, looking at age-related programmatic shifts of tenocytes 1 (Figure 5F–H), while young WT tenocytes 1 exhibited processes such as 'collagen biosynthesis', 'ECM organization', and 'immune cell chemotaxis' (Figure 5I), aged tenocytes 1 exhibited processes related to potential indicators of aging hallmarks such as loss of proteostasis 'response to unfolded protein', 'protein refolding', and 'inflammaging' 'T cell activation', 'immune response' (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5J.

claim: Tenocytes 2 in the young WT tendons exhibited biological processes such as 'macromolecule biosynthetic and metabolic processes', 'collagen metabolic processes', and 'ECM organization'.
source: Regarding programmatic changes of tenocytes 2 in 6 M WT vs DTR (Figure 5K), FEA analysis from the DEGs (Figure 5L and M) showed that tenocytes 2 in the young WT tendons exhibited biological processes such as 'macromolecule biosynthetic and metabolic processes', 'collagen metabolic processes', and 'ECM organization', while tenocytes 2 in the young DTR group exhibited further elevated as well as new processes related to matrix organization and remodeling such as 'ECM organization', 'extracellular fibril organization', and 'ECM assembly' (Figure 5N and O).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5N.

claim: Tenocytes 2 in the young DTR group exhibited further elevated as well as new processes related to matrix organization and remodeling such as 'ECM organization', 'extracellular fibril organization', and 'ECM assembly'.
source: Regarding programmatic changes of tenocytes 2 in 6 M WT vs DTR (Figure 5K), FEA analysis from the DEGs (Figure 5L and M) showed that tenocytes 2 in the young WT tendons exhibited biological processes such as 'macromolecule biosynthetic and metabolic processes', 'collagen metabolic processes', and 'ECM organization', while tenocytes 2 in the young DTR group exhibited further elevated as well as new processes related to matrix organization and remodeling such as 'ECM organization', 'extracellular fibril organization', and 'ECM assembly' (Figure 5N and O).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5O.

claim: Divergent intrinsic programmatic shifts in tenocytes between DTR and aged tendons might dictate the divergent healing responses that are observed in these models.
source: These divergent intrinsic programmatic shifts in tenocytes between DTR and aged tendons might also dictate the divergent healing responses that are observed in these models.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed differences in tenocyte programming.

claim: Young WT tenocytes 1–3 exhibit both autocrine and paracrine signaling.
source: Young WT tenocytes 1–3 exhibit both autocrine and paracrine signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Tenocytes 1 exhibit high communication strength as both sender and receiver.
source: Tenocytes 1 exhibit high communication strength as both sender and receiver, tenocytes 2 is the predominant sender but exhibits low intercellular communication strength as a receiver and tenocytes 3 exhibits high communication strength as a receiver but low strength as a sender (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion resulted in substantial shifts in tenocyte autocrine and paracrine communication.
source: Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion resulted in substantial shifts in tenocyte autocrine and paracrine communication (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6A-F.

claim: Five signaling pathways (CHAD, LIFR, NECTIN, CADM, EPHA) were identified exclusively in the 6 M WT group.
source: Five signaling pathways (CHAD, LIFR, NECTIN, CADM, EPHA) were identified exclusively in the 6 M WT group, while four signaling pathways (IL6, SEMA3, NOTCH, and FGF) were expressed only in the 6 M DTR group (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Four signaling pathways (IL6, SEMA3, NOTCH, and FGF) were expressed only in the 6 M DTR group.
source: Five signaling pathways (CHAD, LIFR, NECTIN, CADM, EPHA) were identified exclusively in the 6 M WT group, while four signaling pathways (IL6, SEMA3, NOTCH, and FGF) were expressed only in the 6 M DTR group (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Thbs3-Sdc1, Thbs2-Sdc4, Thbs2-Sdc1, and Thbs2-Cd47 ligand-receptor interactions were decreased in tenocytes 1–3 with depletion.
source: More specifically, we identified that Thbs3-Sdc1, Thbs2-Sdc4, Thbs2-Sdc1, and Thbs2-Cd47 ligand-receptor interactions were decreased in tenocytes 1–3 with depletion (Figure 6F), suggesting that this interaction may be important for maintenance of tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6F.

claim: Natural aging results in an almost complete loss in tenocyte communication compared to 6 M WT.
source: In contrast to altered communication in response to DTR, natural aging results in an almost complete loss in tenocyte communication compared to 6 M WT (Figure 6G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6G-L.

claim: Tenocytes 1 and 2 exhibited a loss of both autocrine and paracrine communication with aging.
source: Tenocytes 1 and 2 exhibited a loss of both autocrine and paracrine communication (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6H.

claim: A majority of the signaling pathways were expressed only in the 6 M WT group, suggesting that with natural aging there is a substantial and widespread loss of tenocyte-tenocyte communication.
source: A majority of the signaling pathways were expressed only in the 6 M WT group, suggesting that with natural aging there is a substantial and widespread loss of tenocyte-tenocyte communication (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6I-K.

claim: SPP1 and WNT pathways were present only in the aged group in both an outgoing and incoming pattern.
source: Interestingly, SPP1 and WNT pathways were present only in the aged group in both an outgoing and incoming pattern (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6J and K.

claim: There was a loss of THBS signaling with natural aging, including Thbs3-Sdc4, Thbs3-Sdc1, Thbs2-Sdc4, Thbs2-Sdc1, and Thbs2-Cd47.
source: Finally, we also identified a loss of THBS signaling with natural aging, including Thbs3-Sdc4, Thbs3-Sdc1, Thbs2-Sdc4, Thbs2-Sdc1, and Thbs2-Cd47 (Figure 6L), which was very similar to the ligand-receptor interactions lost with depletion (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cell communication analysis presented in Figure 6L.

claim: Aging results in broad decline in tenocyte-tenocyte communication.
source: Taken together, aging results in broad decline in tenocyte-tenocyte communication, and future work will define whether decreased and altered communication between the remaining tenocytes may drive further degeneration beyond that observed at 21 M B6.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Aging impairs tendon homeostasis, increases the risk of degeneration and the frequency of injury, and diminishes healing capacity after injury.
source: Aging impairs tendon homeostasis, increases the risk of degeneration (Riel et al., 2019; Teunis et al., 2014) and the frequency of injury, and diminishes healing capacity after injury (Ackerman et al., 2017; Teunis et al., 2014; Houshian et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Age-related tendon changes are associated with impaired dynamic stability and increased risk of falling.
source: In addition, clinical studies have shown that age-related tendon changes are associated with impaired dynamic stability and increased risk of falling, factors that significantly increase both morbidity and mortality (Onambele et al., 2006; Tomlinson et al., 2021; Karamanidis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of Scleraxis-lineage cells in the adult tendon mimics age-related impairments in cellular density, ECM structure, composition, and material quality.
source: Moreover, we demonstrated that depletion of Scleraxis-lineage cells in the adult tendon mimics age-related impairments in cellular density, ECM structure, composition, and material quality.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of a critical mass of biosynthetic tenocytes, or biosynthetic tenocyte function initiates a degenerative cascade in tendon.
source: More specifically, we have demonstrated that loss of a critical mass of biosynthetic tenocytes, or biosynthetic tenocyte function initiates a degenerative cascade in tendon.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the effects of tenocyte depletion.

claim: It is the decline in cell density and the accompanying loss of cell function itself that drives age-related tendon degeneration, rather than age-related programmatic shifts.
source: This is particularly striking as it demonstrates that it is the decline in cell density and the accompanying loss of cell function itself that drives age-related tendon degeneration, rather than age-related programmatic shifts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of the depletion and aging models.

claim: Preventing the loss of biosynthetic tenocytes is a critical intervention point for maintaining tendon structure-function.
source: Moreover, we have identified preventing the loss of biosynthetic tenocytes (whether via apoptosis or other mechanisms) as a critical intervention point for maintaining tendon structure-function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the importance of biosynthetic tenocytes.

claim: This model results in sustained cell depletion, thus allowing assessment of the long-term impact of Scleraxis-lineage cell deficiency.
source: Indeed, this model results in sustained cell depletion, thus allowing assessment of the long-term impact of Scleraxis-lineage cell deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing sustained depletion over time.

claim: This model likely depletes any 'progenitor' cell populations due to the use of non-inducible Scx-Cre, further inhibiting any potential cellular rebounding post-depletion.
source: It is important to note that this model likely depletes any 'progenitor' cell populations due to the use of non-inducible Scx-Cre, further inhibiting any potential cellular rebounding post-depletion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic design of the model.

claim: With Scleraxis-lineage depletion, there is an acceleration of the natural age-related tendon cell loss.
source: We observed that Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion resulted in almost identical cellular density with older (12 M old) and geriatric (31 M old) tendons, indicating that with depletion, there is an acceleration of the natural age-related tendon cell loss.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the quantitative data showing similar cell densities.

claim: There may be mechanisms that maintain a minimum level of cellularity and prevents complete cell loss.
source: However, the fact that Scleraxis-lineage depletion in young animals results in a comparable decline in cellularity suggests there may be mechanisms that maintain a minimum level of cellularity and prevents complete cell loss, although these mechanisms remain to be defined.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that cell density does not decline to zero.

claim: The recapitulation of many established hallmarks of tendon aging, including altered ECM structure, organization, and material quality, further supports the utility of defining the consistent underlying mechanisms between DTR and aging to define previously unappreciated drivers of age-related tendon pathology.
source: Moreover, the recapitulation of many established hallmarks of tendon aging, including altered ECM structure, organization, and material quality (Connizzo et al., 2013; Gehwolf et al., 2016; Dunkman et al., 2013; Sugiyama et al., 2019; Ippolito et al., 1980; Watanabe et al., 1994; Watanabe et al., 1997), further supports the utility of defining the consistent underlying mechanisms between DTR and aging to define previously unappreciated drivers of age-related tendon pathology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of the depletion and aging models and supported by citations.

claim: Scleraxis-lineage cells are required to directly regulate the synthesis and maintenance of multiple GPs and PGs, which are crucial to maintain tendon structure-function.
source: Consistent with declines in high-turnover rate proteoglycans and glycoproteins with aging in other tissues (Choi et al., 2020; Ewald, 2020; Ariosa-Morejon et al., 2021; McCabe et al., 2020), these classes of proteins were decreased in both aged and young depleted tendons, demonstrating that Scleraxis-lineage cells are required to directly regulate the synthesis and maintenance of multiple GPs and PGs, which are crucial to maintain tendon structure-function, since their decrease results in significantly impaired collagen fibril organization and biomechanical properties.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proteomic data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Scleraxis-lineage cells are a 'master-regulator' of multiple ECM-related proteins during tendon homeostasis.
source: In contrast, we demonstrate that Scleraxis-lineage cells are a 'master-regulator' of multiple ECM-related proteins during tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proteomic data showing the effects of Scleraxis-lineage cell depletion.

claim: COCH expression is observed in the spiral ligament of the inner ear, and Coch-/- results in degeneration of this ligament.
source: Interestingly, COCH expression is observed in the spiral ligament of the inner ear, and Coch-/- results in degeneration of this ligament (Kommareddi et al., 2007), further supporting the potential importance of this molecule in maintenance of tendon structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Age-related declines in ECM biosynthetic function have also been identified in mouse and human skin fibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, age-related declines in ECM biosynthetic function have also been identified in mouse and human skin fibroblasts (Solé-Boldo et al., 2020; Salzer et al., 2018), thus, future work will focus on establishing and disrupting the mechanisms that drive age-related declines in biosynthetic tenocyte number and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GBP2 exhibits host-defense and anti-microbial functions.
source: While there are no studies that have assessed the function of GBP2 in tendon, other studies have shown that GBP2 exhibits host-defense and anti-microbial functions (Tretina et al., 2019; Kutsch and Coers, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tenocytes 1 may play a role in the immune defense response of tendons after injury.
source: Based on the innate immune and defense response BPs of tenocytes 1, in addition to their biosynthetic capacity, it could be speculated that this subpopulation may play a role in the immune defense response of tendons after injury.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed biological processes of tenocytes 1.

claim: Sdcn4 is required for muscle development, homeostasis, and healing after injury.
source: While this specific pathway has not been extensively studied in tendon, previous work has shown that Sdcn4 is required for muscle development, homeostasis, and healing after injury (Cornelison et al., 2004; Rønning et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The tenocytes that remain in aged tendons demonstrate programmatic skewing, including an increased pro-inflammatory signature and loss of proteostasis.
source: First, the tenocytes that remain in aged tendons demonstrate programmatic skewing, including an increased pro-inflammatory signature and loss of proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: These programmatic shifts may drive subsequent degeneration at timepoints beyond those included in this study.
source: While these shifts are not necessary for homeostatic disruption, as evidenced by comparable disruptions in DTR tendons in the absence of this skewing, it is possible that these changes drive subsequent degeneration at timepoints beyond those included in this study.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed programmatic shifts in aged tenocytes.

claim: 31 M B6 tendons exhibit substantial increases in ECM disorganization, relative to DTR.
source: Consistent with this, 31 M B6 tendons exhibit substantial increases in ECM disorganization, relative to DTR.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative data on collagen dispersion.

claim: The pro-inflammatory signature and loss of proteostasis may be a precursor to subsequent tenocyte senescence.
source: Moreover, while no enrichment of senescent markers was observed in aged tenocytes, it is possible that the pro-inflammatory signature and loss of proteostasis may be a precursor to subsequent tenocyte senescence, which could be an important driver of additional tendon degeneration.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed programmatic shifts in aged tenocytes.

claim: Aged tendon resident macrophages demonstrate similar shifts in biological processes toward a response to protein unfolding, suggesting this may be a conserved feature of tendon cell natural aging.
source: Finally, in addition to the unique programmatic shifts observed in aged tenocytes vs. the young depletion model, aged tendon resident macrophages demonstrate similar shifts in biological processes toward a response to protein unfolding, suggesting this may be a conserved feature of tendon cell natural aging.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the single-cell RNA sequencing data on macrophages.

claim: 22 month-old tendons heal in a mechanically inferior manner, relative to young tendons, and fail to form the provisional ECM needed for successful healing.
source: Consistent with impaired healing capacity in many aged tissues (Ackerman et al., 2017; Browder et al., 2022; Sgonc and Gruber, 2013; Yamaguchi et al., 2021), we have previously shown that 22 month-old tendons heal in a mechanically inferior manner, relative to young tendons, and fail to form the provisional ECM needed for successful healing (Ackerman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: DTR tendons demonstrate improved healing capacity relative to age-matched WT repairs.
source: In contrast, the cells that remain in DTR tendons display programmatic shifts associated with enhanced remodeling capacity. Moreover, DTR tendons demonstrate improved healing capacity relative to age-matched WT repairs (Best et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Homeostatic disruptions including decreased cell density and altered ECM composition, quality and organization are not of central relevance to the quality of the tendon healing response.
source: Finally, these data highlight the surprising finding that homeostatic disruptions including decreased cell density and altered ECM composition, quality and organization are not of central relevance to the quality of the tendon healing response, suggesting a de-coupling of the mechanisms that regulate homeostasis and healing capacity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of homeostatic disruptions and healing outcomes in the two models.

claim: The Scx-DTR model targets all Scleraxis-lineage cells.
source: One limitation of the study is that the Scx-Cre; DTR F/+ targets all Scleraxis-lineage cells, and the Scleraxis-lineage is known to contribute to tissues in addition to tendon (e.g. bones and muscle) (Agarwal et al., 2017; Yoshimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors and supported by citations.

claim: The Scleraxis-lineage is known to contribute to tissues in addition to tendon (e.g. bones and muscle).
source: One limitation of the study is that the Scx-Cre; DTR F/+ targets all Scleraxis-lineage cells, and the Scleraxis-lineage is known to contribute to tissues in addition to tendon (e.g. bones and muscle) (Agarwal et al., 2017; Yoshimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.
